title: Separate HTTP response body ownership from connection reuse
applies_when: A Go net/http resource-lifetime lead claims a missing response Body.Close necessarily opens a new TCP connection on every call, or proposes cleanup inside a helper that returns a live body to its caller.
lesson: Trace who owns the response and test Close separately from connection reuse. After successful Client.Do, a helper consuming or rejecting the response owns cleanup; defer Close before status/read-error returns. Reading a successful body to EOF can already permit keep-alive reuse, so a real missing Close does not establish the claimed throughput or connection-growth mechanism. Use actual httptest HTTP responses with a close tracker for success, empty, non-200 and truncated reads, plus a two-request connection-count control. Preserve the valid cleanup finding while correcting the unsupported explanation.
avoid_when: If a helper returns the successful body, its caller may own Close; unconditional defer would invalidate that API. The observed EOF/reuse control is Go 1.25.10 HTTP/1.1 with a local server, not all transports, streaming bodies, live cloud behavior or a memory/throughput measurement. A Close count proves only the reached response paths. PR publication is not maintainer acceptance or full-repository qualification.

evidence.note: The standard library assigns response-body cleanup to the caller of a successful Do. Its reuse guidance is not a guarantee that every missing Close prevents reuse.
sendUsage consumes or rejects the response internally and never returns its body; non-200 returns before reading. ReportUsage invokes this helper periodically, not on every filesystem operation.

Real HTTP/native Go: four Close-count cases fail on unchanged production and pass with the one-line fix; the successful EOF connection-reuse control passes on both. Full usage package and focused five-repeat race checks pass, not all JuiceFS packages.
Published Ready cleanup correction with reproduction scope and omitted full-suite/lint checks disclosed. No measured throughput or whole-system resource-growth claim.
